content: Pulmonary embolism is one of the leading causes of death related to pregnancy. Accurate diagnosis in pregnant patients is essential to prevent the risks associated with untreated pulmonary embolism, as well as to avoid unnecessary anticoagulant therapy and unwarranted preventive measures. Imaging techniques used to diagnose pulmonary embolism may perform differently in pregnant patients due to their younger age, fewer comorbidities, and altered physiology. Additionally, pregnant patients have largely been excluded from diagnostic studies, which complicates the evaluation of these imaging methods. The objective of this study was to assess the diagnostic accuracy of computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA), lung scintigraphy, and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) for detecting pulmonary embolism during pregnancy. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE and Embase databases up to July 2015. Citation searches, find similar functions, and reference list reviews were also utilized. Experts in the field were consulted to identify studies that might not have been indexed. The inclusion criteria for the analysis required studies to involve consecutive series of pregnant patients suspected of having pulmonary embolism. These patients must have undergone one of the index tests (CTPA, lung scintigraphy, or MRA) and had either clinical follow-up or pulmonary angiography as the reference standard. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed by two independent reviewers. Investigators of potentially eligible studies were contacted to obtain missing data. In the primary analysis, inconclusive results from the index tests were treated as negative if no treatment for pulmonary embolism was initiated, and as positive if treatment was administered. A total of 11 studies were included in the review, comprising four studies on CTPA, five on lung scintigraphy, and two that evaluated both methods. These studies provided data on 695 CTPA results and 665 lung scintigraphy results. No studies on MRA met the inclusion criteria. Lung scintigraphy was performed using various techniques across the studies. The overall risk of bias and concerns about the applicability of the studies were high, given the research question. There was also significant heterogeneity in study methods, which precluded the possibility of conducting a meta-analysis. All studies used clinical follow-up as the reference standard, but none were designed in a way that could reliably identify false-positive results. Consequently, sensitivity and negative predictive value were the only valid measures of test accuracy. For CTPA, the median negative predictive value was 100%, with a range of 96% to 100%. The median sensitivity was 83%, ranging from 0% to 100%. For lung scintigraphy, the median negative predictive value was also 100%, with a range of 99% to 100%. The median sensitivity for lung scintigraphy was 100%, with a range of 0% to 100%. The median frequency of inconclusive results was 5.9% for CTPA (ranging from 0.9% to 36%) and 4.0% for lung scintigraphy (ranging from 0% to 23%). The overall median prevalence of pulmonary embolism in the included studies was 3.3%, with a range of 0.0% to 8.7%. The authors concluded that both CTPA and lung scintigraphy appear to be suitable for excluding pulmonary embolism during pregnancy. However, the quality of the evidence necessitates caution in adopting this conclusion. Significant limitations were identified, including the use of suboptimal reference standards, assumptions made in the analysis regarding inconclusive test results, and the inability of the included studies to identify false positives. It remains unclear which diagnostic test has the highest accuracy. There is a pressing need for direct comparisons of these diagnostic methods, including MRA, in prospective, randomized diagnostic studies.
